## 01 Overview

Zeus, an AI agent, helped design a heavy-lift drone, bought key components, and provided instructions for the build. In six days, the drone delivered its first payload.

We wanted to test whether an AI agent could question requirements and make engineering choices that held up under review. Could it prepare usable instructions for vendors, manufacturers, and other engineers? Could it help find failures before they happened in the physical world?

We found Zeus to be a strong contributor in workloads that were highly meticulous and time-consuming. It ran the hand calculations and simulations for the structural frame ( 3.1 , 3.2 ). It found parts, provided supplier links, and tracked orders ( 04 ). It also wrote the 34-page wiring book the team built from ( 5.1 ). After the flight, the team generated 50 drone designs from the same brief ( 2.1 ).

Its limits were in engineering judgment and communication. Engineers still had to decide when a requirement or rule should change. Zeus could trace its calculations, but it did not always carry critical assumptions into the build instructions ( 06 ).

### 1.1 The setup

The team outlined some boundary conditions: 6 days, a limited materials budget, and an unlimited token budget. The drone was flown under Part 107 as a small unmanned aircraft system, weighing less than 55 lb including the payload.

Three full-time engineers worked on the build. The team had broad engineering experience but little experience building drones.

### 1.2 Project setup

The whole project sat in one central Zeus project, with shared CAD assemblies, a BOM, calculations, and other files. Within the project, engineers could start sessions for different tasks. Users quickly came to anthropomorphize the agents, dubbing them "Project Manager" or "Manufacturing Engineer."

Every project, session, and knowledge base was shared across the entire team, allowing new users to onboard quickly into existing context.

Upon use, it was immediately clear that existing models had highly uneven capabilities. They especially struggled with:

- Engineering judgment. Understanding why a rule or requirement exists, and when a different approach is justified.

- Communicating assumptions. Making sure the conditions behind a calculation reach the people who build the part.

The work fell into three kinds:

- Work the team would have skipped. Zeus made a 34-page wiring book, with every wire length measured from the CAD, in 38 minutes ( 5.1 ). Nobody on the team would have drawn it by hand.

- Work done together. The payload bay went through five reviewed revisions with an engineer in about two hours.

- Broader exploration. The team generated 50 drone designs from one brief after the build, each with its CAD, parts list, and calculations.

## 02 Design

### 2.1 Engineers can now prototype by choosing between dozens of designs

Concepts are cheap for an agent. The team generated 50 drone designs using the same project requirements, steering each toward a different layout, including a hexacopter, a coaxial octocopter, and a frame of folded sheet metal. Designs can also follow abstract constraints, such as "make a quad that can fold into the back of a car." Most designs came back in one to two hours, each with its CAD, parts list, and calculations.

### 2.2 Engineers could track cascading interface changes in an assembly

A large part of the project centered on negotiating interfaces between subsystems.

The team considered replacing a machined aluminum landing bracket with a thicker printed bracket, which required longer clamp bolts. A fit check found the bolt tips and tether eye intersecting the payload plate in CAD. At an engineer's direction, Zeus lowered the payload mount and reran the bolted-joint calculations.

### 2.3 Zeus can make direct edits in connected CAD software, but requires highly detailed instruction

Zeus connected to the team's Onshape document to inspect parts and edit the assembly. Engineers could ask it to import components, change their positions, and update the hardware around them. Zeus saved the changes in Onshape for the team to review. Over the week, one engineer’s chat saved 12 versions of the assembly this way.

However, Zeus struggled with detailed design without concrete instructions, diagrams, and annotations. It could miss the broader intent behind engineering decisions or produce unnecessarily complicated designs.

For the payload-bay swap, Zeus imported the replacement design into Onshape and removed the previous bay from the assembly. It moved the new bay up 1.6 mm to match the revised mounting plate, updated the fasteners, and checked clearances. It then saved the updated assembly as a new Onshape version.

## 03 Analysis and verification

### 3.1 Agents do best with ongoing records of past decisions

Zeus kept a mass tracker through 5 revisions. Every line identified the source of its number: the maker's spec, the CAD, an assumption, or values calculated from formulas based on textbooks such as Roark's and Shigley's. It saved each calculation as a card with its inputs, their sources, its assumptions, and its result.

Can you show all of the calculations for current draw to hover?

### 3.2 Engineers with little simulation experience could identify vibration modes

When a hand calculation could not settle a question, Zeus ran a finite element analysis using its suite of tools. It compared coarse and fine meshes, then checked the result against a hand calculation. On the arms, that turned up a problem nobody had asked about. The team asked whether the arms and legs were strong enough. They were, but the arms' fundamental frequency (the frequency at which the arms would vibrate uncontrollably) fell within the band of frequencies generated by the props at hover.

## 04 Sourcing

### 4.1 Zeus helps teams buy and track the parts they bought

This capability was one of Zeus's most beloved features. Zeus helped source parts throughout the build. It told the team what to buy, provided supplier links, and tracked deliveries. Team members could check the chat to see what had been purchased and when it would arrive, without asking each other. A human engineer handled a few orders, including the waterjet plates, while working with Zeus.

When a part could not arrive in time, Zeus found an alternative. For example, the Mauch current sensor had to ship from Germany and could not arrive in time. Zeus moved current sensing onto the power board, which had a built-in sensor.

## 05 Assembly and testing

### 5.1 Zeus does not have hands, but can make instructions for those that do

Zeus made the work instructions the team printed out and built from. Before the bench test, the engineers asked for a wiring diagram with the correct lengths, connectors, and clamps. In 38 minutes, Zeus made a booklet with every wire length measured from the CAD. The booklet included an overview of the whole system and a page for each step. It listed the parts, tools, and cut lengths, with numbered instructions and checks to pass before moving on.

But Zeus could not yet help with the physical assembly. That is only a matter of time.

> The documentation quality of Zeus is incredible. Zeus made detailed diagrams, gave thorough explanations, and kept track of every important decision that was made at any time. Build lead

The documentation quality of Zeus is incredible. Zeus made detailed diagrams, gave thorough explanations, and kept track of every important decision that was made at any time.

### 5.2 Zeus’s context and constant availability made it a strong project manager

Zeus kept one decision log, one mass tracker, and one parts list for the whole team. That made Zeus the fastest way to get up to speed. Team members often asked Zeus to read every chat and give them a status update.

The same record kept the team aligned in person. Team members worked from the same printed sheets at the bench. When someone joined a new part of the build, they asked Zeus for an update on that work.

## 06 Limitations and deficiencies

Zeus's analysis was a strength of the build. It chose useful methods, checked calculations, and kept results traceable. The limits the team encountered concerned engineering judgment and how assumptions reached the people making parts.

### 6.1 Engineering judgment

Engineering judgment includes understanding why a rule exists and when departing from it is justified. A requirement can reflect a physical limit, a manufacturing constraint, or a choice that no longer applies.

Zeus tended to pursue the stated requirements rather than question whether a simpler approach could remove them. Engineers still had to make that call. The difficulty was knowing when to change a rule and how to justify the change.

### 6.2 Communicating assumptions

Zeus could trace a result through its inputs and decisions. But an assumption in the analysis also needs to reach the manufacturing instructions. For one landing-leg bracket, the analysis assumed a solid part without making the need for 100% infill clear to the person printing it. The bracket was printed at 10% infill and broke too easily.
